title: Math You Actually Need

character.name: The Number Sage
character.tagline: Fear not the Greek letters — they're just fancy hats on simple ideas.

oneLiner: The small, useful slice of linear algebra, calculus, and probability that AI actually runs on.
analogy: Imagine AI math as a kitchen. Linear algebra is the countertop where you lay out all your ingredients (numbers) in neat trays called vectors and matrices. Calculus is the taste-test: you take a sip, decide 'needs more salt,' and nudge the recipe in the right direction — that nudge is a gradient. Probability is you shrugging and saying 'it's PROBABLY chicken' when the dish is ambiguous. You don't need to be a Michelin chef; you need to know which knob to turn and which way.
objectives: Recognize vectors and matrices as the containers AI uses for data and parameters.
Understand a gradient as 'which direction reduces the error' — the heart of learning.
Read basic probability (likelihood, distributions) without panic.
Know just enough notation to follow tutorials and papers.
keyConcepts: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; a matrix is a grid of them. Nearly all AI data (an image, a sentence, a user) becomes a vector.
The dot product measures how aligned two vectors are — it quietly powers similarity, attention, and recommendations.
A derivative/gradient tells you the slope of the error surface; gradient descent walks downhill to reduce error.
Probability describes uncertainty; models often output a probability distribution over possible answers rather than one certain answer.
You optimize a 'loss function' — a single number saying how wrong the model is — by nudging parameters to make it smaller.

keyTerms.plain: A row of numbers. Think of it as coordinates describing a thing.
A spreadsheet of numbers the model multiplies things by.
An arrow pointing toward 'less wrong.' Follow it downhill.
The model's report card: one number for how badly it messed up.
A map of how likely each outcome is.

scenarios.scenario: You're building a feature that finds 'similar' movies. Each movie is represented as a vector of numbers.
scenarios.question: Which operation most directly measures how similar two movie vectors are?

options.label: The dot product / cosine similarity between the vectors
Counting the letters in the movie titles
Taking the derivative of one vector

scenarios.explanation: Similarity between vectors is measured with the dot product (or cosine similarity, its length-normalized cousin). This same idea underlies embeddings, search, and attention.

quiz.question: In machine learning, what is a 'gradient' used for?
options: Coloring charts with a smooth fade
Telling the model which direction to adjust its parameters to reduce error
quiz.answer: Telling the model which direction to adjust its parameters to reduce error
quiz.explanation: A gradient is the slope of the loss with respect to the parameters. Gradient descent nudges parameters 'downhill' to reduce error — the core of how models learn.

quiz.question: What is a loss function?
options: A single number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are
A type of neural network layer
quiz.answer: A single number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are
quiz.explanation: The loss summarizes error as one number. Training = minimizing the loss by adjusting parameters.

quiz.question: How is most real-world data (an image, a word, a user) represented for AI?
quiz.explanation: Almost everything is turned into vectors (lists of numbers) so math can operate on it — pixels, tokens, and user features all become vectors.

quiz.question: What does a probability distribution describe?
options: The exact single correct answer, always
How likely each possible outcome is
The number of layers in a model
quiz.answer: How likely each possible outcome is
quiz.explanation: Distributions capture uncertainty — models often output probabilities across many options rather than one certain answer.

quiz.question: Do you need advanced, proof-heavy math to START building with AI?
options: Yes, a PhD is required before touching any tool
No — a working intuition for vectors, gradients, and probability is enough to begin
quiz.answer: No — a working intuition for vectors, gradients, and probability is enough to begin
quiz.explanation: You can be productive with intuition for the core ideas and deepen the math over time. Understanding beats memorizing notation.
